In Proverbs 30, Agur expresses his weariness and ignorance, questioning God's nature and name. He recognizes that God's word is true and a shield, warning against adding to it. Agur asks for two things: to be kept from falsehood and to have neither poverty nor riches, but enough to avoid temptation. The chapter lists four types of people who displease God: those who disrespect authority, those who are self-righteous, those who are prideful, and those who harm the poor. It also presents a series of threes and fours illustrating various aspects of life: things that are never satisfied (Sheol, a barren womb, land, fire); things that leave no trace (an eagle, serpent, ship, and a man with a virgin); things that make the earth tremble (a slave becoming king, a fool with food, an unloved woman finding a husband, a maidservant displacing her mistress); and small but wise creatures (ants, rock badgers, locusts, and lizards). The chapter emphasizes the importance of contentment, faithfulness, and trusting God. It warns against foolishness, slander, and anger, highlighting that God's wisdom is far more valuable than worldly pursuits.

This sermon, based on Isaiah 52:13-53:12, focuses on the "Fourth Servant Song" and its fulfillment in Jesus Christ. It highlights the themes of humiliation and exaltation, disbelief and rejection, and their application to believers. The sermon is structured around five stanzas, with a central focus on Isaiah 53:5: "he was pierced for our transgressions".

The sermon begins with the servant's exaltation, noting that he will act wisely and be lifted up. However, this exaltation is connected to his suffering and disfigurement. The "lifting up" refers to both his glorification and crucifixion, emphasizing the paradox of victory through humiliation. The servant's suffering leads to the cleansing and redemption of many nations. Despite this, the sermon acknowledges widespread disbelief. The servant grew up humbly, without beauty or majesty, and was despised and rejected. This rejection stemmed from people's desire for a different kind of Messiah.

The sermon concludes with applications for believers. Believers should not reject God's gifts based on their form, and they should find comfort in knowing that Jesus understands suffering. The sermon also stresses that Christians should follow Jesus' example of self-denial, rather than seeking worldly comfort or glory.

Proverbs 25 contains wisdom applicable to leaders, neighbors, and individuals. For leaders, it emphasizes the importance of curiosity, investigation, and surrounding oneself with righteous advisors, not those who are self-promoting. It is the glory of God to conceal things, but the glory of kings to search them out. For neighbors, the teaching stresses loving one's neighbor, resolving conflicts directly, and avoiding gossip and slander. It encourages treating others as you would want to be treated. A word fitly spoken is invaluable, like gold, and a wise reproof should be given and received with a listening ear. The teaching also warns against false witness, which is as dangerous as a weapon.

The text advises against gluttony and overstaying one's welcome, and promotes generosity and kindness towards enemies. Self-control is essential, as a person without it is like a city without walls. The best news to share is the gospel of Jesus Christ. Christians should avoid aligning with the immorality of the culture. Jesus is presented as the embodiment of these principles, having lived them perfectly.

Proverbs 24 emphasizes the importance of living according to God's wisdom, which includes discernment and skill for living well. Wisdom, honesty, obedience to authority, diligence, and hard work are key to a good life. Envy is one of the things that can derail a person from a life of wisdom. It is unwise to envy those who do not live according to integrity and wisdom, because they have more trouble than one might think. Wisdom is the skill to live right, understanding is seeing connections between actions and consequences, and knowledge is knowing the truth. Fools are not patient for these things and seek immediate gratification.

Other things that can derail a wise life include planning to do evil, devising folly, and scoffing at what is right. It is also important to not give up in the face of adversity. God is watching over our souls, understands our intentions, and will reward those who are faithful. The righteous may fall, but they will rise again, while the wicked will be ruined when they stumble. Do not rejoice when an enemy falls, because God may see this as scoffing. Instead, fear the Lord, honor those in authority, and do not join with those who do otherwise. Be diligent, plan ahead, and do your work. The fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom, and we need to humbly ask the Lord to write wisdom on our souls.

Instead of behavior modification, parents should teach their children to trust the Lord, pray, think, and grow in God's love. Discipline should be done with love and patience, not with an overly strict, micromanaging approach.

Generosity to the poor is also emphasized, as is staying out of debt. Those with wealth should share and not exploit the poor, as God is gracious and generous to those who are spiritually poor. People should treat others as they would want to be treated and should strive to live with integrity, humility, and justice.

Proverbs 19 contrasts two ways of living: a broad path of destruction and a narrow path of wisdom. The broad path is characterized by folly, crooked speech, and a lack of integrity, often pursued by those who are wealthy and powerful. This path is marked by desires without knowledge, hastiness, and actions that lead to ruin. Those on this path may experience the consequences of their choices and blame God. In contrast, the narrow path is marked by integrity, understanding, and a fear of the Lord. This path emphasizes gaining sense and understanding to discern good and evil.

Key aspects of the narrow path include: being slow to anger, overlooking offenses, and being a peacemaker. Additionally, the narrow path involves being generous to the poor, keeping God's commandments, and disciplining children. It's also characterized by listening to advice, accepting instruction, and understanding that one's plans are subject to God's purpose. Ultimately, the fear of the Lord is the foundation for this path, leading to a life of integrity, respect, and security. The chapter underscores that the choices people make have real consequences.

The teaching highlights that a wise person seeks understanding, listens before speaking, and is careful with their words.

Key points include:
• The power of the tongue: Words can bring life or destruction. A fool's words can lead to conflict and ruin, while gossip is like poison.
• The need for humility and listening: One should listen to understand, not just to formulate a response. It's important to consider all sides of a story before making a judgment.
• Seeking refuge in God: When facing a crushed spirit, the Lord is the ultimate refuge and source of wisdom.

Arrogance is an abomination to the Lord, while steadfast love, faithfulness, and the fear of the Lord atone for iniquity and turn one away from evil.

The chapter also contrasts worldly values with Godly wisdom. It is better to have a little with righteousness than great revenues with injustice, and better to have a lowly spirit with the poor than to divide the spoil with the proud. True wisdom involves giving thought to the word of God and trusting in Him. Additionally, wise speech is gracious and persuasive. The chapter also warns against doing what seems right in one's own eyes, as that path leads to death. Finally, living a righteous life, being slow to anger, and ruling one's spirit are hallmarks of wisdom and can lead to a long life.

Proverbs 14 is a collection of 35 two-line proverbs that contrast wisdom and foolishness, offering practical insights into human nature and life. The chapter falls into a broader category of "two ways" literature within the Bible, presenting two distinct paths: the way of the wise and the way of the foolish.

Key teachings in Proverbs 14 include:
* The Importance of Wisdom: The chapter emphasizes the value of wisdom and discernment, contrasting the wise, who are cautious and turn away from evil, with the foolish, who are reckless and careless. The wisdom of the prudent is to discern their way, while the folly of fools is deceiving.
* The Fear of the Lord: Walking in uprightness and fearing the Lord are associated with wisdom, while devious ways show a despising of God. The fear of the Lord is a fountain of life that helps one turn away from the snares of death.
* Consequences of Foolishness: The chapter illustrates the negative consequences of foolish behavior, such as being quick-tempered, dishonest, and deceptive. 
* The Power of Words: Proverbs 14 highlights the impact of speech, noting that the mouth of a fool brings a rod for his back, while the lips of the wise preserve them. A truthful witness saves lives, but a false witness is deceitful.
* The Two Paths: The chapter contrasts two paths in life: the way of the righteous and the way of the wicked. The way of the wicked leads to destruction, while the way of the upright flourishes. There is a way that seems right to a man, but its end is the way to death. The house of the wicked will be destroyed, but the tent of the upright will flourish.

* Listening to Instruction: The chapter begins by emphasizing the importance of listening to instruction and rebuke. A wise son heeds his father's teaching, while a scoffer does not. Ignoring instruction leads to poverty and disgrace, while heeding reproof brings honor.
* The Power of Words: Proverbs 13 highlights how one uses their speech can affect their life. Those who guard their mouths preserve their lives, while those who speak carelessly face ruin. The righteous speak truth, while the wicked bring shame.
* Diligence and Work Ethic: The chapter contrasts the diligent with the sluggard. The soul of the diligent is richly supplied, while the sluggard craves and gets nothing. Wealth gained hastily will dwindle, but whoever gathers little by little will increase it.
* Righteousness and Wickedness: The proverbs contrast the outcomes of righteousness and wickedness. Righteousness guards the blameless, while sin overthrows the wicked. The righteous hate falsehood, while the wicked bring shame. Disaster pursues sinners, while the righteous are rewarded with good.
* Wealth and Inheritance: The chapter touches on the topic of wealth, noting that a good man leaves an inheritance for his children's children while the wealth of a sinner is stored up for the righteous.

* Consequences of Wickedness: Selfish, wicked behavior ultimately leads to harm, distrust, sorrow, and misery.
* Practical Advice: The proverbs offer practical advice for daily living, covering topics such as speech, work, relationships, and financial matters. For example, it advises against dishonesty, laziness, and being overly prideful.
* The Power of Words: Proverbs 12 highlights the importance of truthful and wise speech, noting that truthful lips endure forever while lying tongues are fleeting. The tongue can bring healing or harm.
* Marriage: The chapter touches on marriage, noting that an excellent wife is a crown to her husband.

title: Fear Not! Look Up & Listen
subtitle: Isaiah
speaker: Rev. Jason Van Bemmel
more_info:
The sermon, based on Isaiah 51:1-16, addresses the fears and anxieties of God's people and calls them to a life of faith. The sermon can be outlined as follows:

* **Introduction**: The sermon begins by acknowledging that believers often struggle with fear, losing perspective and acting out of self-protection rather than faith. The people of God in Isaiah 51 were afraid of being conquered, exiled, and abandoned by God.
* **Three Calls to Listen**: God calls his people to listen three times, emphasizing the importance of hearing and receiving His word:
 * Verse 1: To those who pursue righteousness and seek the Lord.
 * Verse 4: To God's people, His nation.
 * Verse 7: To those who know righteousness and have God's law in their hearts.
* **Looking Back**: The sermon urges listeners to remember God's past faithfulness.
 * The call of Abraham and Sarah and God's promise to multiply them.
 * God's creation of the heavens and the earth.
 * The Exodus from Egypt and God's parting of the Red Sea.
* **Looking Forward**: The sermon encourages listeners to look forward to God's future promises:
 * The coming of a law of justice and salvation for all people.
 * The final day of judgment and redemption.
* **Looking Up**: The sermon calls for prayerful and passionate engagement with God, not passive acceptance. The "frozen chosen" aside contrasts this with a passive, unemotional faith.
* **Speaking God's Word**: The sermon concludes by emphasizing the importance of speaking God's word:
 * To oneself, to combat fears and anxieties.
 * To other believers, to encourage them.
 * To the world, sharing the gospel.

title: That the Gentiles May Share in Our Joy
subtitle: Walking with Jesus in the Word
speaker: Rev. Jason Van Bemmel
series: Walking with Jesus in the Word
more_info:
Sermon by Stan Long on Romans 15:1-13 from December 5, 2024.

Pastor Long outlines three points from Romans 15:1-13: a call to be a people of harmony, a call to be a people on mission, and a call to be a people of power.

A call to harmony. This point emphasizes the need for believers to be united and live in harmony with one another, despite differences in cultural backgrounds or practices. God calls us to forbearance, being concerned about one's neighbor, and using Christ as an example of yielding oneself to others. The church should demonstrate how different voices can blend together in harmony. 

A call to be on mission. Jesus came as a servant to the circumcised, confirming God's promises to the patriarchs, and opening the way for Gentiles to come to faith. God's desire was always to include the Gentiles and that the barriers of the Old Testament were always meant to be temporary. The Old Testament passages here support the idea that God wants all nations to embrace His covenant. We must not be ashamed of the gospel and appreciate all people.

A call to be people of power. The Holy Spirit is the power of God in the lives of believes. The Holy Spirit is God and gives believers assurance, illumination of the word of God, and the power to obey God. The power of the Spirit is not just to bless the believer, but to empower them to bless others. God gives us hope, joy, and peace from the Holy Spirit.

This sermon on Isaiah 49:17-26 explores the true meaning of Christmas joy, contrasting fleeting happiness with the enduring joy found in faith in Jesus Christ. Pastor Jason differentiates between "merry," "happy," and "joy," emphasizing the latter's connection to a deeper sense of purpose and fulfilled hope rooted in God's covenant. Finally, it calls listeners to actively cultivate and share this lasting joy, focusing on Christ and living by faith and in hope.

title: What God Says About Suicide
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info:
911 - Imminent Danger
988 - Suicide & Crisis Lifeline

This sermon presents a biblical perspective on suicide, emphasizing that while the term is absent from Scripture, the act is consistently portrayed as sinful and contrary to God's design for life, which is sacred and entrusted to Him alone. It refutes the notion that suicide is an unpardonable sin, affirming that salvation through faith in Christ secures eternal life regardless of how one dies, and that God's love, as revealed in Romans 8:38–39, cannot be severed by death or any other force. The message addresses the profound grief of survivors, acknowledging their pain, guilt, and isolation as legitimate yet not reflective of personal failure, while urging the church to offer compassionate, holistic support that integrates both spiritual truth and practical care. It highlights the spiritual warfare at play, warning that suicidal thoughts often stem from the enemy's lies, and calls believers to resist despair by anchoring hope in Christ, who conquered death and offers abundant life. Ultimately, the sermon calls all who are struggling or grieving to find refuge in Jesus, the only true source of lasting hope and healing.

The Head Covering by Josiah Bongioanni offers insights into questions that arise from 1 Corinthians 11 in a style that mixes analytical thinking with numerous stories and historical quotes. In an age where the church is continually moving away from Biblical principles and neglecting divine commands, this book draws attention to an oft neglected question, aiming to call Christians away from following wayward society and determining what God's Word says so as to follow the Bible seriously.

subtitle: The Faith Debate
speaker: Troy Skinner
more_info:
This stream of The Faith Debate radio show doing an in-studio recording session replaces the lack of a worship service live stream for July 20th.

The panel interacts over a WallBuilders event in DC, things that are non-negotiable for Christianity vs. what are adiaphora, and how to vet churches.

Panel:
Troy Skinner. Pastor, Household of Faith in Christ
Daniel Razvi. Pastor, Church That Meets at Imran's
Imran Razvi. Founder, Conquered By Love Ministries

Topic Breakdown:
Section 1- The WallBuilders organization hosted a "Pastors Briefing" at the US Capitol where a dozen speakers (nine members of Congress) shared the political status of things "inside the beltway" with 100 pastors over the course of two days. What was the big takeaway from attending this short conference?

Section 2- What must churches and Christians get right when it comes to questions of abortion, marriage, sin, and understanding the gospel?

Section 3- Expanded thoughts on the Defense of Marriage Act (which proved to be a paper lion) & the demonic Respect for Marriage Act (which actually disrespects biblical marriage).

Section 4- Continuing to define "marriage", "woman", "man", and things related to DOMA and RFMA. Also, talk of polygamy, divorce, being unequally yoked, and the purpose of marriage.

Section 5- Thoughts about Kinism (inter-ethnic marriage), marriage ceremonies, and items that are "borderline red flags" when vetting a local church.

This video contains 5radio shows. All 5 are available as audio podcasts.

title: The Once-for-All Sacrifice
speaker: Rev. Jason Van Bemmel
more_info:
The Once-for-All Sacrifice
Hebrews 10:1-18
Maundy Thursday 2024

The Repetition of Futility: The Old Testament Sacrificial System
Day after day, Year after year. Daly sacrifices and the Day of Atonement. Never finished. Never sitting. Always.
~450 years in the Tabernacle. ~400 years in Solomon's Temple (990-587). ~500 years in the Second Temple. (517 BC – 70 AD)
So, WHY? The purpose of the Old Testament sacrificial system
To be a constant reminder of sin and the need for redemption

What made Jesus' sacrifice better?
He's infinitely more valuable – The Son of God vs Animals
He was sincerely and perfectly obedient – truly spotless – Sinlessly perfect and complete
He was willing – He freely offered Himself

What did Jesus' sacrifice accomplish?
Perfected for all time those who are being sanctified
 Positional sanctification vs Process of sanctification
No longer any offering for sins

How are we changed by His sacrifice?
Set free from guilt and shame
Set free from the endless cycle of futility
Set free to obey from the heart in love and sincerity

title: The Most Damaging Thing in the Christian Home
subtitle: Marriage Matters Conference
speaker: T. H. Moore
more_info: The sermon identifies hypocrisy—the dissonance between outward religious performance and inward reality—as the most damaging force within the Christian home, drawing from James 3:17 to contrast divine wisdom, which is pure, peaceable, and genuine, with the deceitful nature of pretense. It defines hypocrisy as a form of spiritual dissembling, rooted in the Greek term for 'actor' or 'one who conceals,' and illustrates how it manifests in actions, speech, and attitudes, particularly when believers live double lives—upright in church yet inconsistent at home. The sermon warns that such duplicity breeds rebellion and distrust in children, undermines the believer's testimony, and severs genuine relationship with God, citing biblical examples like Lot and the Pharisees to underscore the inevitable exposure and spiritual consequences of living falsely. Ultimately, it calls for radical authenticity, urging believers to abandon pretense, confess their struggles, and live with integrity in all spheres, so that homes may become genuine reflections of God's truth and bear lasting fruit in the lives of future generations.

title: The Ministry Man
subtitle: Marriage Matters Conference
speaker: Rodger Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical definition of true manhood, calling men to embody self-control, sacrificial love, and spiritual leadership rooted in faithfulness to God and His Word. Drawing from David's life as both a man of great faith and profound failure, it emphasizes that repentance, restoration, and renewed commitment to God enable transformation and divine purpose. The preacher urges men to stand firm in their convictions, guard their homes from worldly influences, lead with humility and courage, and cultivate daily devotion through Scripture and prayer. He warns against cultural relativism, moral compromise, and the erosion of godly masculinity, calling believers to be vigilant, intentional, and Christ-centered in their families and communities. Ultimately, the message affirms that godly manhood is not defined by strength or status, but by surrender to God, integrity, and a lifelong pursuit of righteousness.

speaker: Phillip Bishop
more_info: The sermon centers on the vital responsibility of parents to win their children's hearts for Christ, emphasizing that every behavioral issue stems from a deeper heart problem rooted in sin, not external factors like teachers or schools. Drawing from personal anecdotes from police work and parenting, the message underscores the necessity of consistent, biblically grounded discipline marked by thankfulness, thoughtfulness, transparency, and thoroughness—never in anger or retaliation. The preacher illustrates how to model Christ-like love and accountability, even through creative, structured methods like mock court, to address rebellion while fostering repentance and spiritual growth. Ultimately, the call is to walk in the Spirit, nurture children in the Lord's instruction, and trust that God uses parents to guide their children toward salvation, especially strong-willed ones who, when reached, can become powerful agents of change.

title: Learning to Forgive
subtitle: Marriage Matters Conference
speaker: Rodger Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the transformative power of forgiveness within marriage, rooted in God's unconditional forgiveness through Christ, calling couples to emulate divine mercy by choosing to forgive, forget, and love unconditionally. Drawing from Ephesians 4:32 and numerous biblical examples, it emphasizes that selfishness and unforgiveness are primary destroyers of marital harmony, while intentional kindness, humility, and prayerful reconciliation foster lasting unity. The preacher underscores that forgiveness is not passive but a deliberate act of grace—mirroring God's faithfulness, completeness, and willingness to erase sins as far as the east is from the west—requiring conscious effort to release bitterness and avoid the accumulation of offenses. Through vivid illustrations and personal anecdotes, the message challenges believers to prioritize their spouse's dignity over pride, to treat their partner with the same care they would a guest, and to cultivate a spirit of continual forgiveness, even when repeated offenses occur, echoing Jesus' command to forgive 'seventy times seven.' Ultimately, the sermon presents forgiveness not as a burden but as a pathway to emotional healing, spiritual freedom, and deeper intimacy, grounded in the truth that only through God's grace can marriages endure and thrive.

title: Learning to be Consistent
subtitle: Marriage Matters Conference
speaker: Rodger Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the vital importance of spiritual consistency across generations, illustrating how faith must be actively lived, taught, and modeled to endure beyond the first generation. Drawing from the narrative in Judges 2, it highlights the tragic decline of Israel from faithful obedience to apostasy, attributing this to the erosion of conviction and the failure to pass on enduring spiritual truths. The preacher emphasizes that mere belief is insufficient—parents must embody consistent faith through daily practices, miraculous testimonies, and sacrificial living so that children not only hear about God but see His reality in action. Without deliberate, persistent discipleship, even godly families inevitably drift into compromise and unbelief, leading to spiritual generational collapse. The message calls for intentional, faith-filled parenting that prioritizes God's presence and provision, ensuring that future generations inherit not just beliefs, but a living, transformative relationship with Christ.

subtitle: Marriage Matters Conference
speaker: Rodger Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the transformative power of selfless love and intentional kindness within marriage and family, calling believers to prioritize their spouse's well-being through daily acts of gratitude, respect, and shared experiences. Drawing from biblical principles such as loving others as oneself and the call to think on things that are true, honest, and pure, it emphasizes that genuine Christian living is not confined to Sunday worship but permeates every aspect of daily life. By modeling Christ-like character, parents not only strengthen their marriages but also shape their children's future relationships and spiritual formation. Ultimately, the message calls for a radical shift from self-centeredness to other-centeredness, where the heart is continually given to spouse and family as a living expression of faith.

In lieu of a video of a Household of Faith in Christ sermon, for this week we present this a recording of a live stream of the Faith Debate radio show doing an in-studio recording session.

This behind-the-scenes look makes you a fly on the wall as the panel interviews a Chinese national who lives in Singapore. During our time together we recorded four episodes of The Faith Debate radio program discussing:

Christian conversion in the context of a deeply secular Asian culture, the importance of retaining Chinese culture even in the church, the most offensive part of Christianity in China, the status of the church in China, and misunderstandings between the CCP & churches.

Throughout the discussion there was a unifying thread addressing the implications for growing the Christian church in societies that are either pre-Christian or post-Christian. Due to a technical mishap, the full studio session was unfortunately not recorded.

title: But I Say: Control Your Lust
subtitle: But I Say
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon confronts the modern cultural normalization of sexual immorality by grounding its message in Christ's authoritative teaching in Matthew 5:27–30, where He declares that lustful desire constitutes adultery in the heart, elevating moral standards beyond mere external actions. It emphasizes that while society increasingly celebrates sexual freedom and relativizes morality, Scripture consistently affirms adultery as a grave sin that defiles the heart, destroys relationships, and undermines societal integrity, citing biblical passages from Exodus, Leviticus, Proverbs, and Hebrews to underscore God's unchanging moral law. The preacher warns that unchecked lust, even in thought or glance, is spiritually equivalent to the act, leading to spiritual death, and calls for radical self-discipline—symbolized by Jesus' hyperbolic commands to cut off offending body parts—as a call to mortify sinful desires through intentional separation from temptation, guarding one's thoughts, and cultivating purity through godly habits and relationships. Ultimately, the message balances conviction with grace, affirming that while no sin is beyond God's forgiveness—illustrated by Christ's mercy toward the woman caught in adultery—it demands immediate repentance and a proactive commitment to purity before sin takes root, urging believers to pursue holiness, restore marital intimacy, and maintain a clean heart before God.

title: But I Say: Control Your Anger
subtitle: But I Say
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on Jesus' teaching in Matthew 5:21–26, emphasizing that true righteousness requires mastery over the heart, not just outward actions, with a particular focus on controlling anger as a spiritual discipline. It warns that uncontrolled anger—rooted in pride, impatience, and self-justification—leads to foolishness, judgment, and spiritual harm, contrasting the world's explosive rage with God's righteous indignation, which is slow to develop, swift to dissipate, and specifically directed against sin. Drawing from Scripture and modern psychological insights, the message calls believers to recognize anger's symptoms, remove themselves from provoking situations, replace bitterness with kindness and forgiveness, and actively pursue reconciliation and peace, even with adversaries, as a reflection of Christ's example. Ultimately, it presents the transformation of anger through the power of the Holy Spirit as essential to Christian maturity and the health of the church.

Christian Nationalism: Defining Theonomy

There's an unseemly battle royale taking place among Christian conservatives this year. Some of the fight is over semantics, some is over vision for the future, and some of it (sadly) is due to personality conflict.

The panel spends six episodes attempting to directly expose the issues involved, hoping to forthrightly frame the various dialogs within a biblical context. This is a VERY complex issue that touches upon how to understand what's called Theonomy (in distinction from Theocracy and Sacralism), how understand prophecy (primarily in relation to Postmillennialism, Amillennialism, and Preterism), and how to understand the moniker "Christian Nationalism" (as distinct from Christianity proper, Christendom, and even Sharia Law).

That's a lot to cover. This is episode 1 of 6. The full discussion of six shows is available as one long video on the Rumble channel for Household of Faith in Christ. https://rumble.com/v2kr5kc-video-gg-theonomy-and-christian-nationalism.html

more_info:
Jesus: The Only Way? (Based on John 14:6)
Intro: Why it can be a tough pill to swallow:
Because, We live in a pluralistic society where tolerance reigns and free enterprise competes with new and better ideas rising to the top.

Why It Makes Sense: 
Because:
1) It's recorded in the Scriptures
2) Jesus himself declared it to be so, John 14:6
3) The Apostles make the same bold claim: Peter in Acts 4:12; 
 Paul in 1 Tim. 2:5; John in 1 John 5:11-12
 Note: These statements were not made to drive people away, 
 but intended to provide a clear invitation to all who dare to come.
 John 6:37; John 3:16 and that no one might miss out.
4) Jesus is God - and Possesses all power over us: as Creator, Sustainer, Forgiver, Judge and Savior. Mat.1:23; Col.1:16-17, Luke 5
5a)All roads lead to the judgment seat of Christ, 2Cor.5:10; Jn. 5:22-23
5b) Story of the Famous Babe Ruth who disagreed with the umpire
6a)"Without holiness no one can see the Lord" Heb.12:15, and only Christ has the perfect record to clothe us with moral beauty.
6b)Moral beauty is required to join heaven's celebration and Christ can declare us to be morally beautiful / brand new 2Cor. 5:17
(see also Mat.22:11-13)
7) Lastly, We would all be lost apart from God's love.
And God has no greater way of showing us his love than
giving up his own life, to show us how much he loves us.
APPLICATION: 1) Meditate often on the scars in Christ's hands
so you can daily remember how much God cares for you
2) Just as a river overflows its banks, let God's love overflow to those around you, so they will desire to follow (and keep following) the only one who can lead us to that great celebration that awaits us in heaven.

The Power of Jesus to Give Sight to the Blind, Part 1
John 9:1-23

First, we are going to look at the miracle itself. Then, we are going to look at the various reactions to the miracle. 

1. THE MIRACLE. The miracle is that Jesus gives sight to a blind man (verses 1-7).

The purpose is to display God's works (verses 1-5).

The procedure is anoint and wash (verses 6-7).

The point is that Jesus gives spiritual sight (see verse 39).


2. THE REACTIONS. The reactions prove that miracles do not change hearts (verses 8-23).

The man's neighbors have mixed opinions (verses 8-12). 

The Pharisees denounce Jesus (verses 13-17).

The Jewish leaders launch an investigation (18-23).

title: The Most Important Thing
speaker: Matt Fortunato
more_info:
The Most Important Thing
Romans 10:5-13

Overview
 All of salvation is all of Christ and always will be. Christ is all you need to be right with God (verses 5-8), and faith is all you need to receive Christ (verses 9-11), because Christ is Lord over all people in all places for all time (verses 12-13). His kingdom of redemption knows no boundaries.
 As believers, we are those who submit to Christ's Lordship. We also rejoice in and proclaim His Lordship. We rest in Him and trust in His Lordship instead of things in this world. And, finally, we pray for the fuller and fuller expression of Christ's Lordship in the world. We pray, "Your kingdom come, your will be done."

Outline

Main Message: All of salvation is all of Christ and always will be.

I. Christ is all you need to be right with God (v. 5-8)
 1. There are two kinds of righteousness (v. 5; see v. 4 also!)
 2. The righteousness of faith requires no mediator between you 
 and Jesus (v. 6-7)
 3. The righteousness of faith requires faith in Jesus through the 
 gospel (v. 8)

II. Faith is all you need to receive Christ (v. 9-11)
 1. Genuine faith leads to sincere confession (v. 9a, 10b)
 2. Genuine faith resides in the heart (v. 9b, 10a)
 3. Genuine faith includes knowledge of the truth (v. 9)
 4. Genuine faith loves Jesus, not just gifts from Jesus (v. 11)

III. Because Christ is Lord over all people in all places for all time 
 (v. 12-13)
 1. There is universal equality before Christ (v. 12a)
 2. Based on the universal Lordship of Christ (v. 12b)
 3. And, therefore, there is a universal call to Christ (v. 12c)

title: Christ's Heart for Our Holiness
speaker: Matt Atack
more_info:
Because we know these truths so well, my fear is that we underestimate the degree to which God is concerned for our present holiness. 

In general, we see God's concern for holiness rooted in his justice and nature and law; but then we see the greatest demonstration of God's concern for holiness manifested in Christ crucified for sins and his perfect imputed righteousness, and we think then that:
- because Christ has been made our "wisdom, righteousness, sanctification and redemption (1 Cor 1:30)
- because Christ is "all in all,"
- because Christ said upon the cross, "it is finished," 
- because we are no longer under Law but under grace, God is not so much concerned for our present holiness anymore. 

His commands are more like suggestions than demands. 
A set of instructions for a well ordered life.

You would not say such things out loud. 
But I'm here to tell you that - at some point - your flesh suggested these lies to you, and you swallowed them up, hook, line, and sinker. 

And I know this because you still live like Christ isn't all that concerned for your present holiness. 

You don't know his heart as you should. 
You have to see his heart for your holiness.

September 5th, 2021 - 9:00 am
News Radio 930 WFMD in Frederick, Maryland

After seventeen years of "tweaks" bringing different "seasons" to the Faith Debate show, there was a new tweak beginning with this episode.

At the very start of the program's existence (in 2004) it basically followed an interview format. Then it turned into more of a "talking heads" opinion show; guests have included all worldview traditions, and the conversations spiritedly tackled tough philosophical ideas and hot cultural topics. The show has also had periods when there were no guests, but merely a one man monologue. All of this came together in a brand new way beginning with this edition.

Into the foreseeable future there would be a set panel of local faith community leaders each week. This gave listeners the opportunity to better know exactly who's talking to them and where their motivations are rooted. The issues addressed moving forward continue to be profound, with the dialogue being just as spirited as ever. This represents an exciting new moment in the show's trajectory and hope that listeners continue to see it this way.

more_info: The sermon calls Christians to cultivate a constant posture of gratitude, not limited to Thanksgiving or seasons of blessing, but rooted in the unchanging character of God. It emphasizes that thankfulness is not merely a seasonal sentiment but a divine command and a spiritual discipline essential to the Christian life, grounded in the reality that every good gift comes from God and that true gratitude flows from recognizing His sovereignty, grace, and provision. more_info: The sermon draws a powerful parallel between Nehemiah's call to rebuild Jerusalem's walls and the Christian's responsibility to build spiritually enduring lives, communities, and the Kingdom of God. This building involves nurturing one's own faith through Scripture, prayer, and discipline, while actively strengthening others through encouragement, teaching, and fellowship, recognizing that each interaction either fortifies or undermines spiritual growth. The message warns against spiritual decay caused by physical exhaustion, discouragement from fellow believers, or misplaced focus, urging Christians to remain vigilant, disciplined, and united in purpose. Ultimately, the call is to rise up and build with eternal significance, knowing that every effort will be revealed and tested at Christ's return, when the trumpet will sound and the work of faith will be completed.

This is the 4th show with the same 3 men on the panel. Each episode has opened with commentary on a video from Phil Vischer (creator of VeggieTales). VeggieTales is fine, however the cartoons don't represent Christ the way that most seem to think. Sadly, neither does Phil. Many trust Phil as a biblical voice for the Gospel. But it's actually because of Phil's work on VeggieTales that he can't be a trustworthy voice for advancing the biblical gospel.

Many kids have seen all the videos with their parents laughing alongside them. These animated short stories are examples of good clean fun, highlighting messages of moral behavior. This is good, particularly when compared to most of what passes for children's entertainment these days. Yet, the VeggieTales universe is merely a kindhearted moralistic universe. It's not a Christ-exalting, cross-centered universe.

The body of Christ can never forget, moralism is not the biblical message. The gospel is the biblical message. Vischer's 17-minute political video is well-crafted, advocating his point of view very effectively, but the video doesn't resonate with many followers of Christ because Phil isn't talking to them. At best Phil is talking at them, which is about all that CRT allows. Phil surely means well, but his video offers no solution because Christ is the solution, and Phil's video doesn't offer Him. It's a good snapshot of what's going on in today's world.

title: Let Us Be Content
subtitle: Let Us
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical call to contentment, rooted in 1 Timothy 6:8, where Paul urges believers to find satisfaction in having food and clothing. It highlights how modern consumer culture, digital advertising, and societal pressures foster a pervasive discontent that extends beyond material possessions to relationships, jobs, and even weather, revealing a deeper spiritual issue of idolatry and misplaced priorities. The preacher contrasts this with the example of Paul, who found contentment in both abundance and hardship, demonstrating that true satisfaction comes not from external circumstances but from a heart aligned with God's will and eternity. The message warns against the prosperity gospel's false equation of wealth with godliness, emphasizing that godliness with contentment is the greatest gain, as it invests in eternal rewards rather than earthly accumulation. Ultimately, the sermon calls believers to practice contentment through daily surrender, gratitude, and a focused gaze on eternal realities, trusting that God provides all needs and that true fulfillment is found not in what we possess, but in who we have in Christ.

title: Let Us Choose Judgment
subtitle: Let Us
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical call to cultivate spiritual discernment—defined as the God-given ability to distinguish truth from error, virtue from vice, and what pleases Him from what does not—by grounding decisions in Scripture, a growing relationship with God, and sensitivity to the Holy Spirit. Drawing from Job 34, it emphasizes that true judgment is not self-centered or worldly, but rooted in wisdom, humility, and a desire to honor God, contrasting the natural human tendency toward pride and poor discernment with the mature Christian's capacity to 'think biblically.' The message warns against the dangers of spiritual immaturity, the influence of secular worldviews, and the failure to test all things against Scripture, urging believers to pursue discernment through diligent study, submission to the Spirit, and a love for God that naturally leads to righteous choices. Ultimately, discernment is portrayed not as a mere intellectual exercise, but as a fruit of a deep, loving relationship with Christ, essential for spiritual health and effective witness in a culture lacking moral clarity.

title: Let Us Go Possess It - I Want that Mountain

speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical example of Caleb, who boldly declared, 'Now therefore, give me this mountain,' as a model for believers facing insurmountable challenges in life. It emphasizes that true victory comes not from passive waiting, but from a combination of persistent prayer, faithful anticipation, and active obedience—trusting God's promises while diligently preparing and striving to fulfill His will. The preacher illustrates how Caleb's lifelong commitment to following God, even after decades of waiting, enabled him to conquer the giants in his path, demonstrating that spiritual triumph requires both divine empowerment and human effort. Through personal anecdotes and biblical teaching, the message calls listeners to identify their own 'mountains'—whether in relationships, spiritual growth, or personal goals—and to pursue them with unwavering faith, perseverance, and readiness to act when God's timing aligns. Ultimately, the sermon affirms that God's promises are reliable, His timing is perfect, and victory is attainable when believers ask, wait, and actively engage in the work He has called them to.

more_info: The sermon, drawn from Galatians 6:10, calls believers to seize every opportunity to do good, emphasizing that God has uniquely equipped each person with abilities—no matter how small—to impact others meaningfully. The message highlights the biblical principle of sowing and reaping, affirming that doing good is not only a moral duty but a divine promise, with God guaranteeing reward for faithful service, even when unseen by others. It also stresses the priority of caring for the household of faith, while recognizing that doing good is not optional but essential, for to know what is right and fail to do it is itself sin. Ultimately, the sermon challenges the congregation to move beyond self-centeredness, embrace their responsibility to others, and live with a heart that actively pursues good, knowing that such obedience brings both personal blessing and eternal significance.

title: Let Us Walk in the Spirit
subtitle: Let Us
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical call to 'walk in the Spirit,' emphasizing that true Christian living involves daily surrender to the Holy Spirit, who indwells every believer at salvation. It corrects common misconceptions by affirming that believers receive the fullness of the Holy Spirit at conversion, not in stages, and that spiritual growth is not about receiving more of the Spirit, but allowing Him to have more of us through continual yielding. The message highlights the ongoing spiritual battle between the flesh and the Spirit, urging believers to choose obedience to the Spirit over fleshly desires, which results in the fruit of the Spirit—love, joy, peace, and self-control—as natural outcomes of a Spirit-led life. Walking in the Spirit is portrayed as a dynamic, relational discipline marked by fellowship, direction, wisdom, and spiritual sight, enabling believers to impact others and perceive God's glory even in trials. Ultimately, the call is to daily surrender, obedience to Scripture, and a life of consistent alignment with God's will, where the Spirit's presence is not a mystical experience but a transformative, practical reality.

title: Let Us Reason Together
subtitle: Let Us
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on God's urgent and gracious invitation in Isaiah 1:18—'Come now, let us reason together'—presenting a divine appeal to humanity to confront the reality of sin and embrace the transformative power of divine forgiveness. Rooted in the profound contrast between the indelible stain of sin, likened to scarlet dye that cannot be washed out by human effort, and the miraculous cleansing promised through Christ's blood, which renders the sinner as white as snow or wool, the message underscores the impossibility of self-justification and the necessity of divine intervention. The preacher emphasizes that God's invitation is not merely a suggestion but a timely, authoritative, and loving call to repentance, grounded in the logical and eternal stakes of eternity, urging listeners to choose faith over indifference, knowing that rejecting this offer is not only illogical but spiritually fatal. Ultimately, the sermon calls for a personal, willing response to God's grace—acknowledging sin, accepting Christ's atonement, and embracing the promise of restoration and eternal life, with the solemn warning that refusal leads to judgment, while obedience brings divine blessing.

more_info: This sermon, drawn from Psalm 34, calls believers to a life of intentional and communal magnification of God, rooted in personal experience and divine faithfulness. The message underscores that magnifying God is both a command and a response to His character, requiring not only verbal praise but a transformed life marked by controlled speech, righteous conduct, and dedicated time in contemplation of God's infinite attributes. more_info: The sermon centers on a heartfelt call to spiritual revival, rooted in Hosea 6:1, where the plea 'Come, let us return unto the Lord' is presented as both a divine invitation and a necessary response to the pervasive tendency of God's people to wander from Him. Drawing from the prophetic narrative of Hosea and his unfaithful wife Gomer, the message illustrates how God's people, like Gomer, have turned to idols and worldly pleasures, yet remain deeply loved and pursued by a merciful God who longs for restoration. title: Today's Un-Protestant Church: The Solution
subtitle: Remembering the Reformation 2
speaker: Dr. Paul M. Elliott
more_info:
Today we are airing part two of a message we began on our last program titled "The Un-Protestant Church." This message is part of our series called "Remembering the Reformation."

In part one we saw that the Evangelical church is returning to the dark condition that the organized church was in before the time of the Protestant Reformation. We saw that the pre-Reformation church was built on Biblical illiteracy, and much of the church is returning to that position of Biblical illiteracy today. Expository preaching is absent from most churches, and very few professing Christians read the Bible in any systematic way. We saw, secondly, that the pre-Reformation church was built on emotional experience, and we find the same thing in much of the so-called Evangelical church today.

As we continue this message today we shall see that the pre-Reformation church was also built on pluralism, and that it was built on man's word, not God's Word. These things also true in much of the church today.

Today's message concludes with a question: What needs to change in order for the Bible-believing church to become truly Protestant, truly the church of the Reformation, once again? Stay tuned for the answer.

title: Lesson 9: Godly Sorrow
speaker: Joel Porcher
more_info:
We need to understand the importance of sorrow:
• Sorrow is the natural response that we feel within to the various challenges and failures we experience in a fallen world. 
• Sorrow is an important emotional that we should expect to experience on a regular basis. 
• Sorrow can be used by God to accomplish good in us. 
• Sorrow can be used by Satan to cripple us and cause us to become essentially paralyzed in our Christian walk.
• If we rarely feel sorrow, then we are likely dealing with some form of self-deception, because we sin daily and are constantly in need of forgiveness and restoration to fellowship with God and others.
• The presence of sorrow and then the absence of sorrow do not necessarily mean that we have properly dealt with the root cause of our sorrow.

Three Basic Forms of Church Government
• Anglican/Episcopalian: Establishment: A hierarchy of bishop oversee a group of church within a highly structured denomination (Anglican, Catholic, Mennonite…)
• Presbyterian: Denomination: A synod of elder/pastors form a body that provides policies that govern a group of likeminded church in a denomination. These churches tend to be run by a group of elders who rule by the consent or affirmation of the congregation.
• Congregational: Fellowship: There is no authority structure higher than the local church, meaning that the congregation governs itself under the leadership of a pastor or pastoral team.

Troy Skinner had recently seen a stage play, a musical, that very accurately captures much that is true about life in the world. As the lyrics to "Seasons of Love" tell us, there is both laughter and strife. And our lives can pass us by quickly with meaninglessness, if we're not careful. But "Rent" blends these helpful insights with a troubling outlook on the human condition. For example, these words from the song "No Day But Today":

"The heart may freeze or it can burn. The pain will ease if I can learn there is no future, there is no past. There's only us, there's only this. No other road, no other way, no day but today. There's only yes, only tonight. We must let go to know what is right. No other course, no other way. I trust my soul. My only hope is just to be. There's only now, there's only here. No other path, no other way, no day but today."

Believe it or not, these songs provide the perfect teaser for a Sunday sermon that recaps a previous sermon preached on 2 John 1-11, and then embraces the wonderful theme of community in fellowship that is found in 2 John 12-13.

title: Let Us Adore Him
subtitle: Let Us
speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical call to adore Jesus Christ, emphasizing that true worship arises from a heartfelt desire to be in His presence, as exemplified by the Magi who journeyed great distances to worship the newborn King. Though the phrase 'Let Us Adore Him' is not found in Scripture, the principle is deeply rooted in the narrative of Matthew 2, where the wise men, guided by a star and driven by faith, traveled from afar, knelt before Jesus, and offered valuable gifts, demonstrating worship that transcends comfort and convenience. The preacher contrasts this genuine adoration with the spiritual apathy and consumerism that often overshadow Christmas, urging believers to prioritize intimacy with God over ritualistic or comfortable religious experiences. He highlights that worship is not merely about attending church or performing duties, but about a transformed heart that values God's presence above all, and that genuine devotion is marked by humility, sacrifice, and a recognition of Christ's divine identity. Ultimately, the message calls the church to rekindle its passion for Christ, to see Him not just in the gifts of Christmas, but in the person of the incarnate Son, and to respond with worship that is both personal and public.

more_info: The sermon centers on Hebrews 13:15, calling believers to offer a continual sacrifice of praise to God through the fruit of their lips, emphasizing that true gratitude is not dependent on circumstances but flows from a heart rooted in faith and recognition of God as the source of every good gift. It challenges the notion that praise should be reserved for times of blessing, arguing instead that faith is most evident in praising God during hardship, when trust in His sovereignty transcends emotional experience. The message highlights that praise is not merely internal emotion but a natural, outward expression—like fruit from a living root—that overflows from a life transformed by God's grace and protection, encouraging believers to cultivate gratitude as a spiritual discipline. It further affirms that such praise, along with acts of kindness, is pleasing to God and ultimately benefits the worshipper, as gratitude is not the result of happiness but the source of it, leading to lasting joy and spiritual fulfillment. The sermon concludes with a call to declare this praise boldly and consistently, recognizing that glorifying God is both our duty and our deepest joy.

title: 92: You May Know That You Have Eternal Life

more_info:
In this topsy-turvy world do you wish there was something you could know for sure? We chase answers minds racing. We search for someone we can depend on, we wonder if anyone's listening. We forget what we once thought we'd learned.

Even those who were lost, but now are found, recognize times when they're unsure of just exactly where they are, losing sight of who they are. In times like these we too often seek satisfaction & assurance in things & situations that disappoint & confuse us.

If only I get the right job, then I'll know. If only I find the right spouse, then I'll know. If only I study harder, then I'll know. If only I withdraw "to find myself", then I'll know. If only I had more money, had more time, had more patience, had more luck, had more sense, had more stuff, had more space -then I'd know. If only. Then I'd know. I'd know what I'm supposed to know.

The Christian life sure would be easier if someone would just tell us what we need to know. Maybe they could write it down so that we could refer back to it from time to time & remind ourselves. Maybe it could be a sort of love letter, even. That'd be great. We'd love that. A love letter telling us what we really need to know to really experience living, to really have life. That's what we want. Perhaps. It's what we need. For sure.

In God's perfect providence He's given us just this, through the Apostle John. God's people come together to sing, pray, confess, rejoice, learn, & proclaim. The sermon examines a portion of John's letter of love to his brothers & sisters in Christ.

more_info: The sermon centers on the Eighth Commandment, 'Thou shalt not steal,' presenting it not merely as a prohibition against theft but as a profound moral and spiritual principle rooted in God's character and the sanctity of private property. It argues that modern society's moral vacuum—born from the removal of divine authority in education and public life—has eroded ethical boundaries, leading to widespread justification of theft, from employee shoplifting and tax evasion to systemic exploitation and even governmental redistribution of wealth. The preacher emphasizes that stealing is not only a violation of God's law but a reflection of a self-centered heart that prioritizes personal gain over love and integrity, contrasting the worldly mindset of 'to get is to live' with the Christian ideal of 'to live is to give.' Drawing from Scripture, including Proverbs and 2 Corinthians, it underscores that true righteousness involves restitution, honesty in work, and the recognition that all things belong to God, making even the theft of time, talent, or honor a spiritual offense. Ultimately, the sermon warns that stealing is not only sinful and destructive but also self-defeating, as every act of dishonesty sows seeds of inevitable consequence, reminding believers that 'whatsoever a man soweth, that shall he also reap.'

more_info: The sermon centers on the fifth commandment, 'Honor thy father and thy mother,' presenting it as a foundational moral principle that bridges the commandments of loving God and loving one's neighbor. It emphasizes that honor is not earned through parental perfection but is a divine mandate rooted in God's design for authority, family, and societal stability. more_info: The sermon centers on the fourth commandment—remembering the Sabbath day to keep it holy—presenting it not as a rigid legal requirement but as a profound spiritual principle rooted in God's design for rest, redemption, and remembrance. It emphasizes that the Sabbath, though originally observed on the seventh day, symbolizes more than a specific day of the week; it points to the rest found in Christ, who fulfilled the law and delivered believers from the bondage of sin. The preacher clarifies that while the Old Testament Sabbath was a sign between God and Israel, the New Testament shifts focus to the spiritual reality of Sabbath rest in Christ, which is observed not by law but by faith. The sermon warns against two extremes: legalistic overemphasis on Sabbath rules and the neglect of rest in favor of worldly pursuits, instead calling the congregation to honor the principle of Sabbath by continually remembering Christ's redemptive work. Ultimately, the commandment is not about a day, but about a relationship—resting in God's grace and celebrating His deliverance.

more_info: The sermon centers on the enduring relevance of the Ten Commandments in a culture that increasingly rejects moral absolutes, emphasizing that these divine laws are not obsolete but foundational to a just and stable society. title: Let Us Labor

speaker: Pastor Caleb E. Bottrell
more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical call to diligently labor in faith and obedience to enter into the spiritual rest God provides, contrasting the unbelief of Israel with the believer's present opportunity to experience divine peace. Drawing from Hebrews 4, it emphasizes that this rest is not eternal salvation—already secured by Christ—but a daily, experiential peace found in faithful obedience, prayer, and Scripture engagement. The preacher underscores that rest is not passive or automatic, nor is it found in mere idleness or religious activity; rather, it is the fruit of sustained, intentional effort in following Christ, likened to a lifelong labor that yields deep spiritual satisfaction. Through vivid illustrations—from parenting and work to personal discipline—the message calls the church to reject spiritual complacency and instead pursue a transformative relationship with God, warning that neglecting this labor is a form of contempt toward God's gracious offer. Ultimately, the sermon exhorts believers to embrace disciplined faith, knowing that God sees and rewards their efforts, and that true rest comes only after faithful labor in His will.

more_info: The sermon centers on the biblical call to 'consider one another' in the context of Christian community, emphasizing that this is not a mere command but a loving, intentional invitation rooted in mutual care and spiritual accountability. Drawing from Hebrews 10:24 and other passages, it underscores that believers are to actively observe, know, and engage with one another—not out of obligation, but out of love, with the purpose of provoking one another toward love and good works. The preacher highlights that this responsibility is most powerfully fulfilled in the gathered church, where faithful fellowship, exhortation, and personal investment counteract the danger of spiritual apathy and isolation. Through practical examples—such as comforting the faint-hearted, warning the unruly, and supporting the weak—the message calls the congregation to intentional, Christ-centered relationships that reflect the Holy Spirit's role as advocate and encourager. Ultimately, the urgency of this charge is grounded in the approaching day of judgment, when such opportunities for mutual encouragement will no longer exist, making present fellowship a sacred duty.

title: The Bread of Life - Eating Christ's Flesh
subtitle: I AM
speaker: Dr. John McKnight
more_info:
When we eat bread, we take into our bodies by way of mouth a substance made of flour, water and other ingredients. These ingredients contain nutrients that are needed by the human body. That raw mixture, baked in an oven, becomes the bread that we devour. By chewing we begin to break down the baked ingredients, and digestive enzymes continue this process until the nutrients are extracted from the bread, absorbed by the digestive tract and transmitted via blood to every part of the body. These are assimilated and transformed into the very flesh of the person; prolonging life and vitality.
When Jesus said “I am the bread of life,” (John 6:35), He was saying that He is the source of spiritual life and vitality. His hearers saw Him and heard Him, but were unable to digest and assimilate the spiritual, life-giving content of His Word. Why?

title: What happens when a Christian sins?
speaker: Dr. Dennis Leatherman
more_info:
Sin is the worst thing in the world.
God does not overlook sin.
A mistake and sin are 2 different things:
- A mistake is inadvertent.
- Sin is deliberate.
What happens when a Christian sins?
1. Sin brings God’s chastisement.
	- Chastisement is a correction, not punishment (vengeance);
Jesus was punished for our sin on the cross!
	- 3 ways He chastens us:
		- With the Word.
		- With the rod.
- With removal.
2. Sin costs us our joy.
3. Sin will quench the work of the Holy Spirit in my life.
4. Sin closes God’s ears to our prayers.
5. Sin has consequences on others besides the sinner.
6. Sin destroys our testimony.
What’s the remedy for sin?
1. Confess. - Not informing God about what you did, but agreeing with Him about it.
2. Forsake. – Get it out of your life.
3. Forget. – Get up and go on living for God!

title: As Wicked Men Increase
subtitle: Jude
speaker: Dr. John McKnight
more_info:
Apostasy is the departure of an individual or a group of individuals from the body of truth they once professed to believe. Apostasy from the truth that God revealed through the prophets, apostles and Christ was well underway shortly after Christ’s ascension into heaven. Writers of the New Testament addressed this matter (I Timothy 2; II Peter 2; Jude, Galatians 1:8).
Such apostasy is the subject of Jude’s epistle. Whereas his intention was to write of the salvation that he and his readers shared in common (v. 3), that purpose was preempted by the presence of apostasy, so that he wrote instead regarding apostates and the response God’s people must make to them.
Jude describes the apostates. First, they turn God’s grace into lasciviousness, or license for immorality. And, they deny our Sovereign and Lord and Savior, Jesus Christ.
For the encouragement of God’s remnant, Jude offered three illustrations from history. This showed that apostasy is nothing new, that God knows how to deal with apostates, and that He is not remiss to do so.

title: The Parable of the Sower
subtitle: BattleFocused Sergeant's Time
speaker: Robert Sims
more_info:
In the Parable of the Sower, Jesus reveals several strategies which the enemies of Christ use to accomplish Satan’s goals. See Matthew 13:1-23, Mark 4:1-20, and Luke 8:1-15.

I believe the primary interpretation of the parable concerns fruitfulness of God’s Word in a person’s life, rather than it being restricted to a discourse on who gets into heaven or not.

The parable tells a story about a person who sows seed, and the seeds fell in four specified environments: the wayside, on rocky ground, among thorns, and in fertile soil. Jesus explains that the seed is the word of God, and the four soils represent those who hear the preaching of the word.  In relating the parable to spiritual warfare, Jesus expressly states that Satan removes the word from the hearts of those who do not understand its meaning (at the wayside). Although Jesus does not describe the devil’s participation any further, I believe that the whole of scripture provides ample evidence that the devil is at work throughout the full story.

more_info: After preaching and healing in other towns and villages of Galilee, Jesus returned to what Matthew describes as 'his own city' at this point in his life, Capernaum.  He was evidently staying again at the home of Andrew and Simon, and word soon spread that he had returned.  A great crowd gathered, and Jesus preached the Word to them.  Four men came to the house, carrying a paralyzed man on a pallet. When they couldn't even approach the door because of the great crowd, they might have turned back, but instead, they climbed the steps to the roof, uncovered a portion of it, and lowered their friend into the midst of the crowded scene.  Jesus, seeing their faith, declared to the paralytic, NOT "Arise and walk," as we might expect, but rather, "Son, your sins are forgiven you." This was too much for the scribes, who were present, and they thought to themselves, "Why does this man speak blasphemies, who can forgive sins but God alone?" Jesus, knowing their thoughts, asked them which is easier to say "Your sins are forgiven you," or "Arise, take up your bed and walk?" Clearly, any false Messiah could SAY, "Your sins are forgiven you." It doesn't require any supernatural power to SAY "Your sins are forgiven." "But that you may know that the Son of Man has power on earth to forgive sins," he said to the paralyzed man, "Arise take up your pallet and walk." Immediately the man did so, to the astonishment of all present!  In this message, we emphasize that affliction can be a blessing; the determination of this man's friends to help him; the fact that our greatest need is forgiveness; and the power of Christ to forgive sin, to heal with his word, and to know men's thoughts.

title: Healing, Praying, Preaching
subtitle: Mark Series
speaker: Russ Sukhia
more_info: Immediately after his teaching in the synagogue of Capernaum, and casting a demon out of a man who was present, Jesus went to the home of Simon Peter and his brother Andrew.  There he healed Peter's Mother-in-law, and apparently spent a restful afternoon.  But by sundown (the end of the Sabbath) all those who were sick or possessed came to Him for healing. After what was likely a tiring night of service, we read that Jesus arose a great while before day to go to a secluded place to commune with His Father. But the disciples found Him in the morning, and told Him there were more people seeking Him.  He told them He must go into the next towns and preach there also. He went throughout Galilee, preaching and healing. The chapter ends with Jesus being approached by a leper, in violation of the Ceremonial law. In this passage we note: The supposed "first pope" was married.  Jesus frequently had long seasons of prayer, and so should we. Healing is important, but it is not most important, all those Jesus healed were dead within a few decades. But those who responded in faith to Christ's message live today. Jesus touched the leper. Human life takes precedence over the laws of men, and the presence of the lawmaker supersedes the law. We learned that ministry can be time consuming and inconvenient, and we illustrated it with the conversion of our own Harry and Nelda Ring. Jesus foresaw that the leper He healed would tell everyone what Jesus did, and as a result, Jesus would have to stay outside the city, in desert places, but He healed him anyway. We have a disease worse than leprosy, a sinful nature which cannot be cleansed by human means.

more_info:
What does it mean to fight the good fight ? How about the right fight? Good versus evil? Good policy v. bad politics? Social justice?

How will the Church prevail against the gates of hell?

As an example let's consider a war story:

It was the age of city states, of castles and cities with high walls, when the leaders of a few hundred acres were called kings. In the times of knights in shining armor, mighty war horses, and frightful dragons. Most days arrived and departed without notice, let alone being recorded by history. They merely faded into tall tales, legends and fables. This story is one of those faint visions of very real, very hard days.
One fall day, after a bountiful harvest, the king of one city still wasn't satisfied with his lot and coveted the bounty of his neighbor. His army attacked the city of his former childhood friend, by sheer surprise defeated the knights of his enemy, stole the harvest, took captive the vast majority of the citizens, and claimed all the land of his neighbor’s kingdom.  Make that – former kingdom.
But the defeated king, many of his knights, and quite a few of his peasants managed to escape the rampages of their new enemy. The winter was a hard one. They survived on scraps and the mercy of strangers while they nursed their wounds and dreamed of revenge. They would reclaim what was rightfully theirs in the coming spring. That so-called “king” would pay dearly for his betrayal.
When that spring day finally arrived they all knew the battle plan. Nothing, and nobody, would stop them from seizing the enemy’s city. The gates of the city would never keep them out...

title: 1 - Is Christ Preeminent In You?
subtitle: Christ Preeminent In You
speaker: Dr. Paul M. Elliott
more_info:
The outline of the book of Colossians can be summarized in three words: Christ's preeminence declared, defended, and demonstrated. In chapter one, the Apostle Paul declares the preeminence of Jesus Christ in all things - the Gospel, the creation, the Church, Christian ministry, and the world to come. In chapter two, he defends the preeminence of Christ against Satan's triple threats of worldly philosophy, legalism, and man-made doctrines. In chapters three and four, Paul sets forth the preeminence of Christ as it is to be demonstrated in the life and thinking of every believer.

In chapters three and four, we shall see that the Christian's conduct, character, home life, work, witness, and service - every aspect of our living and thinking - must be a daily, practical demonstration of the preeminence of the Lord Jesus Christ to our fellow believers and the watching world. He must be preeminent in all these things, because He must be preeminent in us.

title: A Reasonable Faith
speaker: Russ Sukhia
more_info:
Perhaps you've seen the ads from the "Freedom From Religion Foundation."  The Foundation is using the catch-phrase, "In Reason we Trust." Other slogans proposed for billboards include: "All religions are fairy tales," and "Too stupid to understand science? Try religion."  Their message is clear: You can believe in Science and reason, or you can believe in God and religion, but you cannot believe in both.  And if you are going to choose one, you'd might as well choose the one that is real.
The Skeptic would say, "Let's be reasonable. People don't walk on water, they don't heal the blind, the deaf and the lame with a word or a touch, they don't feed thousands with a few small fish and a few loaves of bread, and when they die, they stay dead."  We would respond: "That's right, they usually do!  That's what makes the resurrection of Christ so remarkable, and that's why, all over the world, the wonder of the resurrection is still being proclaimed, almost 2000 years after Christ broke the bonds of death."
But God didn't expect even the apostles to accept something as fantastic as the resurrection without evidence.  The God who created our minds gave us reasons to believe.  Our's is not a "Fairy Tale Faith."
As the late Dr. Wilbur Smith put it, "The meaning of the resurrection is a theological matter, but the FACT of the resurrection is a historical matter."  This message looks at the lives and the testimonies of the eyewitnesses of the resurrection, and asks the question, Is it reasonable to believe that men would suffer severe persecution in this life, and the prospect of severe judgment in the next, for affirming what they knew to be a lie, with no prospect of gain?

title: The Ministry of Reconciliation
subtitle: 2 Corinthians Series
speaker: Russ Sukhia
more_info:
There are times when we feel as if our motives have been wrongly judged. The Apostle Paul had to endure occasions where his motives were misjudged and his actions questioned by members of his own spiritual family in Corinth. Perhaps he felt shocked and hurt just as we would in similar circumstances.
Paul had selflessly founded the church at Corinth with Jesus as its foundation. In Paul’s absence while he was ministering and planting churches elsewhere, rivals crept into the church bearing testimonial letters of recommendation, casting doubt upon the authenticity of Paul’s apostleship and questioning his teaching. Judaizers, as these were described, were particularly inflamed by what they perceived to be Paul’s cavalier attitude toward the law of Moses. They were scandalized that Paul taught Gentile believers that they were not bound to keep the ceremonies and ordinances as expressed in the Old Testament for the nation of Israel through scores of generations. They went on to denigrate not only the matter but the manner of Paul’s teaching. Resorting to name calling they said his presence was weak and speech contemptible.
This put Paul in an undesirable position to defend his calling and teaching. Paul was not concerned with what these rivals thought of him but was concerned for the young believers at Corinth. He did not want them to doubt his apostleship because then they would begin to doubt his message. This message was given to Paul from God to teach others the proper way to be in right relationship with Him and to implore them that only through Jesus who knew no sin can we be reconciled to God.

This sermon in part of a 2 Corinthians Series.

more_info:
There is coming a day when all people will have to stand before Jesus Christ to receive their personal, public and eternal judgment; a day when all actions and motives done on earth, whether good or bad, will be revealed and repaid according to their due. In other words as they say we all must face the music!
Though all people are judged based upon their works, no one is saved based upon their works. People are saved based upon repentance and faith alone in Jesus Christ alone. If you have been saved, God has made you a new creation. As God makes us new, desires to strive earnestly to be pleasing to Him develop within us. So God’s saving grace in us compels us to walk in the path of doing good works. But doing good works apart from faith in Jesus Christ is ultimately unacceptable to God because they are wrongly motivated. The fatal flaw is that these works then spring from the heart of a proud rebel instead of out of love for God. And if you don’t love Jesus, you don’t love God!
So on that day will you be ready to face the music?
When you stand before God, and your works are judged, sentence is given and the gavel is lowered, be sure that the Judge who is Jesus has already been judged in your place at Calvary’s cross for your eternal salvation. Otherwise it is only eternal damnation that awaits no matter how many good works are done in your life.

title: Priceless Treasure in a Clay Pot
subtitle: 2 Corinthians Series
speaker: Russ Sukhia
more_info: Have you ever wondered why God did not continue to proclaim his gospel by means of angels, as He did on the night of Jesus' birth?  We are given an answer here: "We have this treasure (the gospel message) in earthen vessels (common clay pots), that the excellence of the power may be of God, not of us." If not angels, why is there not an elite corps of men---powerful, invincible, a "Gospel Green Beret," to command the world's attention?  Instead, God used men like Paul, evidently short of stature, with poor eyesight, whose "bodily presence" was described as "weak," and whose speech was described as "contemptible."  He was "hardpressed," "perplexed," "persecuted," and "struck down." He was, in himself, nothing more than a weak clay pot. But he did not lose heart, because he knew that his "light affliction," which was "but for a moment, was working for him "a far more exceeding and eternal weight of glory."  He ends the chapter with the remarkable statement:  "...the things which are seen are temporary, but the things which are not seen are eternal." In other words, the reality is just the reverse of what most of us think!  We think the real world is the world of steel and brick and coal and oil, the world of trucks and cars and trees and oceans---but in fact, that is the temporary world---the transitory world.  The real world, the PERMANENT world, is the one we can't see.  But to paraphrase the demon Screwtape from C. S. Lewis' Screwtape Letters, thanks to processes we set in place long ago, humans find it impossible to believe in the unfamiliar while the familiar is before their eyes.
